Nauti Buoy
White Paper Report
Submitted to:
American Society of Naval Engineers (ASNE)
For
Promoting Electric Propulsion 2025 Competition (Unmanned)
Howard University
Submitted By
Team: Jefferson Ogbuka (PM),
Greg Hyson, Evan Barker, Elijah Pratt, Irena Silcott-Nanton
March 25, 2025.EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

This final report details the progress of the Tidal Titans, a team of undergraduate mechanical engineering
students, in designing and preparing the Nauti Buoy, an unmanned electric-propelled watercraft for the
ASNE PEP competition. Building on iterative design phases and rigorous engineering analyses, the team
has finalized component selection, structural modifications, and system integration protocols. The hull, a
prefabricated 49-inch fiberglass catamaran, underwent strategic enhancements, including PVC outriggers
for stability and aluminum reinforcements for weight distribution. These modifications were guided by
computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations and buoyancy calculations to ensure hydrodynamic
efficiency.
The propulsion system centers on two Blue Robotics T200 thrusters, selected for their high thrust-to-weight
ratio and compatibility with a 24V 50Ah LiFePO4 battery pack. This battery system, equipped with
integrated thermal management and overcharge protection, was chosen to maximize energy density while
adhering to weight constraints. A Radiolink-based control framework, paired with Arduino
microcontrollers, enables precise remote operation, ensuring responsiveness to environmental variables
such as currents and wind.
With all components procured, fabricated, or modified, the project now enters its final phase: full assembly
and comprehensive testing. Hull adjustments remain iterative, with refinements ongoing to optimize
balance and drag reduction ahead of scheduled water trials. Pending tests include maneuverability
assessments, endurance validation under race conditions, and emergency system audits.
Through this collaborative effort, the Tidal Titans aim to demonstrate the viability of electric propulsion in
demanding marine applications. By addressing technical challenges through structured innovation, the team
strives to deliver a vessel that not only meets competition standards but also advances the broader adoption
of sustainable naval technologies. TABLE OF CONTENTS

1. Introduction
2. The Big Picture -The Nauti Buoy
2.1. The Hull
2.2. The Propulsion System
2.3. Control System
2.4. The Battery Management System
3. CAD And Testing
4. Risk Management
5. Next Steps1. INTRODUCTION

Propulsion systems have been integral to technological progress, powering vehicles, ships, and aircraft
since the industrial revolution. Historically reliant on internal combustion engines (ICEs) fueled by fossil
resources, these systems revolutionized global trade and travel. However, their environmental and
operational drawbacks—chiefly pollution and inefficiency—present challenges in the face of modern
climate and resource crises.
Combustion-based systems emit significant pollutants such as carbon dioxide (CO2), nitrogen oxides
(NOx), and particulate matter, which contribute to global warming, ocean acidification, and air pollution.
These emissions exacerbate climate change and biodiversity loss, necessitating a shift to cleaner,
sustainable propulsion technologies [1]. Furthermore, ICEs suffer from low thermal efficiency, converting
only 25–30% of fuel energy into useful work, with most lost as heat [2]. Their mechanical complexity
introduces further energy losses and operational wear, emphasizing the need for innovative alternatives.
Electric propulsion systems offer a transformative solution, leveraging electric motors powered by batteries
or fuel cells. These systems achieve efficiencies exceeding 90%, far surpassing ICEs [3]. The sustainability
of electric propulsion is amplified when powered by renewable energy sources like solar or wind. Advances
in battery technology, energy management systems, and power electronics have expanded electric
propulsion's applications across industries, including automotive, aerospace, and maritime sectors.
The maritime industry is increasingly adopting electric propulsion to mitigate environmental impacts.
Competitions like the Promoting Electric Propulsion (PEP), sponsored by the American Society of Naval
Engineers (ASNE) and the Office of Naval Research, encourage innovation in electric watercraft design.
University teams are tasked with developing unmanned electric- powered vessels capable of completing a
2-mile race, promoting advancements in energy efficiency, reliability, and autonomous operation.
In response to the PEP challenge, the team will design an autonomous electric-powered watercraft
optimized for performance and sustainability. The design incorporates high-efficiency electric motors,
lightweight materials, and advanced battery management systems to ensure energy optimization. A
streamlined hull minimizes hydrodynamic drag, enabling high speeds while maintaining stability. Thermal
management and structural integrity are prioritized to maintain consistent performance throughout the race.
The team’s target is to complete the race in under 8 minutes, showcasing the capabilities of electric
propulsion in maritime applications. Beyond the competition, this project serves as a platform to explore
cutting-edge propulsion technologies, contributing to sustainable engineering solutions. The PEP competition embodies a pivotal effort to advance electric propulsion in the maritime sector. By fostering

innovation and sustainability, it aligns with broader environmental goals while preparing the next
generation of engineers to develop transformative naval technologies. Through this project, we aim to
demonstrate the potential of electric propulsion to drive sustainable progress in naval engineering.
2. THE BIG PICTURE – The Nauti Buoy
The Nauti Buoy is a lightweight, electric-propelled watercraft engineered for the ASNE PEP competition,
designed to balance speed, stability, and sustainability through advanced marine engineering solutions.
Built around a 49-inch fiberglass catamaran hull (8.22 lbs), the vessel integrates PVC outriggers supported
by aluminum tubing to enhance buoyancy and hydrodynamic efficiency, validated through iterative CFD
simulations. Figure 1 below shows the preliminary build of the vessel with subsystems integrated.
Propulsion is driven by two Blue Robotics T200 thrusters (22.9 lbf total thrust), powered by a 24V 50Ah
LiFePO4 battery system with integrated thermal management and overcharge protection, ensuring optimal
energy distribution for target speeds of 15 mph. Remote operation is enabled by a Radiolink R12DS
transmitter/receiver system and Arduino Mega 2560 microcontroller, refined through firmware updates for
precise control in dynamic marine conditions. Structural modifications, including reinforced interior plates
and vibration-dampening rubber gaskets, remain under iterative refinement to optimize weight distribution
ahead of final assembly and testing. With all components procured and subsystems tested, the project
advances toward comprehensive hydrodynamic trials, endurance validation, and race simulations,
positioning The Nauti Buoy as a benchmark in sustainable marine innovation aligned with ASNE’s vision
for eco-conscious naval engineering.

Figure 1: The Big Picture - Nauti Buoy2.1. THE HULL (Design and Build Processes)

The Tidal Titans selected a hull with a multihull-inspired design for their unmanned watercraft after an indepth evaluation of hydrodynamic efficiency, stability, and weight distribution. By comparing various hull
designs, including monohulls, trimarans, and hydrofoils, the team concluded that the chosen structure
offered the best balance of reduced drag and enhanced stability — both critical for achieving the
competition’s minimum target speed of 15 mph.
The hull features a single open interior yet incorporates a wider, catamaran-like outer profile, providing
stability benefits typically seen in multihull designs. This shape helps reduce wetted surface area,
minimizing hydrodynamic resistance compared to traditional monohulls. Computational Fluid Dynamics
(CFD) simulations supported this advantage, revealing a drag force of 66N at the target speed and a power
requirement of approximately 737W to sustain it. Constructed from lightweight fiberglass and weighing
just 10 pounds, the hull enhances maneuverability and propulsion efficiency. To guide the design decision,
the team employed a Pugh matrix analysis, where the selected hull excelled in speed efficiency and stability
— two of the most critical evaluation criteria.
To enhance performance and accommodate the hull’s 72-pound weight capacity, the team is implementing
several modifications. Outriggers are being added to improve weight distribution and balance while keeping
drag to a minimum. Internal and external plates will help centralize key components like the battery, cooling
system, and electronics, ensuring even weight distribution and reducing instability. The dual Blue Robotics
T200 thrusters will be securely mounted to the bottom of the PVC outriggers using custom aluminum
mounts, delivering the necessary thrust to counteract drag while maintaining redundancy. Additionally, a
ventilated plastic cover will shield internal components while promoting effective heat dissipation, which
is crucial for sustaining battery and thruster performance.

Figure 2: Hull Preparation and Assembly in Machine shopThese modifications align with best practices in naval engineering, integrating hydrodynamic refinements,

modular component design, and efficient thermal management. The team has already performed CFD
simulations to evaluate the impact of these adjustments, ensuring they enhance overall stability, efficiency,
and performance. Moving forward, additional CFD modeling will be conducted to refine the design further,
ensuring the watercraft meets competition standards while advancing sustainable propulsion technology.
Initial CFD Analysis (Baseline Hull)
A multiphase flow simulation was conducted in ANSYS Fluent to evaluate the hydrodynamic performance
of the unmanned watercraft’s baseline hull. The Volume of Fluid (VOF) model was employed to capture
air-water interactions at the free surface, with the following boundary conditions:
• Domain: 24,000 mm (length) × 7,000 mm (height) × 5,000 mm (width).
• Inlet: Velocity = 6.7 m/s (15 mph), free surface level = -0.075 m.
• Outlet: Pressure outlet, free surface level = -0.075 m.
• Symmetry: Half-boat model to reduce computational load.
• Mesh: Polyhedral mesh with local refinement near the hull (81,325 cells).
The simulation stabilized after 435 iterations, yielding a drag force of 66 N and a drag coefficient
of 0.0368 (Figure 3). The required power to propel the boat at a velocity of 6.7m/s, considering the
calculated drag force and accounting for 60% system efficiency is 737W.
Figure 3: Drag force plot: Baseline hull (66 N)
Updated CFD Analysis (Modified Hull) – Propulsion System Choice
Following structural modifications—PVC outriggers, aluminum 6063 mounts, and interior steel plates—a
revised CFD analysis was performed to assess hydrodynamic impacts. The updated model retained the VOF
multiphase framework but incorporated the new geometry (Figure 4). From this analysis, the drag force
increased to 82.7N due to the outrigger-induced turbulence. The peak pressure at the bow of the boat rose by 18%, while flow separation at the stern diminished. This 25% drag increase necessitated reevaluation

of propulsion requirements. The team selected two Blue Robotics T200 thrusters (14.8lbf each, 65.8 N) to
deliver 131.7 N of total thrust, exceeding the revised minimum requirement of 82.7N (18.6lbf) and
ensuring robust performance under variable conditions.
Figure 4: Drag force plot comparison: Modified hull (82.7 N).
2.2.THE PROPULSION SYSTEM (Integration)
Following the updated CFD analysis for the modified hull, the team chose two T200 Blue Robotics
Thrusters for propulsion. To optimize thrust efficiency and reduce unnecessary weight, the team has revised
the original mounting configuration for the thrusters. Instead of utilizing a back mount, the thrusters will
now be attached beneath the sealed, hollow 4-inch PVC outriggers, which are connected to the hull via
rectangular aluminum tubing. This strategic placement ensures proper thruster spacing, prevents thrust
interference and improves overall propulsion effectiveness. Additionally, this placement allows the team to
maximize the available space on the hull, which is particularly important given the compact size of the
vessel.
This design adjustment offers several key advantages. Firstly, eliminating the back mount reduces excess
structural weight, contributing to an improved thrust-to-weight ratio. Secondly, the lower positioning of the
thrusters within the water column enhances directional control and propulsion efficiency, minimizing
surface turbulence and energy loss.2.3.THE CONTROL SYSTEM

The Tidal Titans' electric watercraft integrates a robust control system based on sound engineering
principles to achieve real-time controllability and optimal power management. Figure 5 presents a System
Block Diagram of the control system.
Figure 5. System Block Diagram
The system employs a Radiolink transmitter and receiver as the primary control interface, making use of
closed-loop signal processing to ensure precise motor command execution with minimal latency. Power
delivery is following a strictly engineered plan, with propulsion coming from a 24V primary battery through
an isolated high-current bus and isolated 12V lithium batteries separately powering control and cooling to
preclude ground interaction and enhance reliability.
Voltage regulation is controlled through a high-efficiency buck converter with dynamic load compensation
to supply stable power with high rates of current changes. The drive system for the thrusters utilizes fieldoriented control software electronic speed controllers, housed in high-current XT90 connectors to reduce
power loss and react instantaneously to signal inputs. Thermally sensitive switching logic powers cooling
fans strategically placed to maintain optimal operating temperatures by utilizing calculated airflow patterns
taking into account component layout and heat dissipation rates.
Every aspect of hardware build shows consideration engineering. The IP67-rated weatherproof housing not
only protects against the environment but also incorporates shielding to keep electromagnetic interference to a minimum. Cabling within the unit follows best practice in high-vibration environments, with major

signal routes separated to reduce crosstalk. Parallel power supply with derating accommodates all the
components operating within safe tolerances, and the modular design facilitates simple maintenance and
fault location.
This system is an example of balanced electromechanical design, where theoretical principles—whether
Kirchhoff's circuit laws or thermal dynamics—are employed to achieve strong, competition-level
performance. The result is a watercraft that demonstrates how foundational engineering principles, when
properly applied, can yield straightforward solutions to what could have been tough technical challenges.
2.4. THE BATTERY MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (BMS)
The development of an efficient and reliable power system is essential for the performance of the
autonomous vessel. The BMS plays a critical role in monitoring battery health, ensuring safe operation, and
optimizing power delivery to meet the propulsion system's demands. This report presents a comprehensive
analysis of the selected battery, its integration with propulsion components, and the supporting electrical
systems necessary for safe and effective operation.
A LiFePO4 battery was chosen due to its superior cycle life, thermal stability, and high energy efficiency
compared to other lithium-ion chemistries. The Newport 24V 50Ah battery was selected for its ability to
deliver sufficient power to meet the propulsion system's energy demands. With the propulsion system
requiring approximately 737W to maintain the target speed of 15 mph, the Newport battery's 1.2
kWh energy capacity ensures the vessel can sustain this output for the duration of the race. This capacity
also provides an energy buffer to account for unexpected fluctuations in load or environmental conditions.
The battery's integrated BMS enhances system reliability with built-in protection features such as
overcharge, over-discharge, and overcurrent protection, safeguarding the system from power
inconsistencies that could impact performance. The BMS also ensures proper cell balancing, maintaining
even voltage distribution to maximize energy efficiency and extend battery life. Its temperature monitoring
system further prevents overheating by adjusting performance to maintain safe thermal conditions during
prolonged operation. These combined features ensure the battery can reliably support the propulsion
system, contributing to stable performance throughout the competition.
3. CAD and TESTING
A Computer-Aided design model was developed using Autodesk Fusion 360 for design, planning, and
simulation purposes. The RC boat hull was captured and created in the CAD model visually by referencing different image views of the actual hull. Once the RC hull was captured in the 3D model, hull modification

components were added to the model by utilizing provided STEP files from manufacturers for the aluminum
railings, PVC pipes, L brackets, bolts, and T200 thrusters. Sourcing manufacturer STEP files allowed more
accurate planning of the design construction by allowing virtual tests and simulations prior to procurement.
This static stress simulation examines the structural integrity of an aluminum 6061 railing intended to secure
an outrigger to the main hull of a naval system. The simulation simplifies the overall design in order to
isolate and focus on the stress behavior of the railing under anticipated operational loads.
Figure 6. Static Stress Analysis of Aluminum 6061 Railings
Multiple simulations were run to observe the railings' performance under varying loads. Two principal
forces are used in Figure 5: a 250 N vertical load in the Z direction to replicate the weight of the outrigger,
and a 100 N horizontal force in the X direction to approximate the push from onboard motors installed
beneath the outriggers. The maximum stress observed is approximately 17.728 MPa, located near the joint
where the railing connects to the hull, suggesting this region bears the highest combined load. The
information from these simulations informed reinforcements needed at stress concentration points. The
aluminum brackets used in the design are capable of withstanding this stress without exceeding their yield
strength, ensuring structural integrity under these conditions.
Testing Plan for ASNE PEP Competition
To ensure the performance, reliability, and safety of our unmanned electric-propelled watercraft, a series of
critical tests have been conducted, with additional evaluations planned. Initial tests were performed in the
lab, where the thrusters were placed in separate buckets of water to assess their functionality and power
draw. Subsequent testing involved using the university's swimming pool to evaluate the fully assembled watercraft's efficiency, maneuverability, and structural integrity, ensuring compliance with competition

requirements.
Completed Tests:
1. Dryness Test
This test evaluated the boat's waterproofing by conducting a dry rehearsal. The hull was carefully inspected
for leaks or breaches in its waterproofing system. Any identified gaps or holes were sealed with epoxy to
maintain the boat's integrity. The hull successfully passed the test with no leaks detected.
2. Battery Management System (BMS) Testing
The BMS underwent extensive testing to confirm its ability to regulate voltage, prevent overcharging, and
manage thermal conditions. The step-down converter integration was assessed to ensure optimal power
delivery while minimizing energy losses. Real-time monitoring of the State of Charge (SOC) and State of
Health (SOH) will be conducted using diagnostic tools to optimize battery performance and lifespan overall.
3. Buoyancy and Stability Assessment
Buoyancy tests were carried out to confirm the vessel's ability to remain afloat under varying payloads.
Stability evaluations ensured the watercraft maintains an even keel, preventing capsizing under sudden
movements or external disturbances.
4. Control System and Remote Kill Switch Validation
The reliability of the remote kill switch was tested to verify its ability to immediately shut down propulsion
in emergency scenarios. Signal range and response time will be analyzed to ensure safe remote operation.
5. Structural Load and Stress Testing
The mechanical durability of mounting brackets, outriggers, and propulsion supports will be tested under
simulated forces. This will verify that all structural elements can withstand operational stresses without
failure.
6. Battery Performance and Endurance
A runtime assessment was performed to determine the battery efficiency under continuous operation. The
initial battery performance test involved connecting the two thrusters to the battery and placing them in
separate buckets of water to evaluate the system's setup and power draw. This preliminary test provided
valuable insights into the system’s ability to sustain peak performance throughout the race.
Tests to be completed by March 28th, 2025:7. Maneuverability and Steering Control

The propulsion system’s response to control inputs will be evaluated through a series of turning radius tests.
The effectiveness of differential thrust steering will be measured, ensuring precise navigation without the
need for a rudder. Data will be collected on agility and directional stability under various load conditions.
8. Speed and Acceleration Tests
The maximum achievable speed will be measured using GPS tracking. Acceleration tests will be conducted
to evaluate thrust efficiency and propulsion response. These results will inform potential optimizations in
power distribution and hull hydrodynamics.
9. Environmental and Temperature Testing
The system’s performance under varying temperatures and environmental conditions will be analyzed to
ensure reliability in different weather scenarios. Heat dissipation efficiency of the BMS and propulsion
system will be assessed to prevent overheating during prolonged operation. These comprehensive tests will
ensure the watercraft is competition-ready, optimizing safety, efficiency, and performance for the ASNE
PEP event.
4. RISK MANAGEMENT
The Nauti Buoy's design integrates a comprehensive risk management strategy that addresses structural,
electrical, hydrodynamic, and operational hazards through proactive engineering solutions and redundant
systems. Structural Risks were a primary concern due to the significant dynamic loads anticipated during
competition. To mitigate potential failures, the team conducted iterative FEA simulations on key loadbearing components, particularly the aluminum 6061 mounting brackets and PVC outrigger joints. These
simulations identified stress concentrations near fastener holes, which were addressed by incorporating
gasket sheets and switching to larger diameter fasteners to improve load distribution. Waterproofing
measures included epoxy-sealed joints, gasket sheets for thruster mounts, and buoyant PVC outriggers.
These solutions were validated through dedicated dryness and buoyancy tests to ensure the vessel’s
integrity.
Thermal Management was approached using both active and passive cooling methods. The LiFePO4
battery pack’s integrated BMS provides cell-level monitoring, ensuring thermal stability during operation.
Additionally, two redundant 12V fans, controlled by NTC thermistors, provide active cooling to prevent
overheating during prolonged operation. This cooling system was tested through continuous stress testing
in the lab, simulating conditions exceeding the race duration to confirm reliability.To enhance Operational Safety, the control system was equipped with both RF and hardwired emergency

kill switches, enabling immediate shutdown in case of system malfunctions or emergencies.
These combined measures effectively mitigate identified risks while ensuring multiple layers of protection
against unexpected failures. The team will conduct final validation during open-water testing, ensuring
system interactions remain stable and reliable under real-world race conditions.
5. NEXT STEPS
To further advance The Nauti Buoy’s performance and expand its applications in marine engineering,
several strategic enhancements could be pursued. Integrating rudders alongside the existing thruster-based
steering system presents an opportunity to reduce energy consumption during maneuvers. By offloading
directional control from thrusters to hydrodynamically optimized rudders, power could be reallocated to
propulsion, improving overall efficiency. Computational simulations could compare rudder configurations
to identify designs that minimize drag while maximizing responsiveness. Autonomy and AI-driven
navigation represent another critical frontier. Implementing machine learning algorithms trained on realworld hydrodynamic and environmental data could enable adaptive pathfinding, allowing the vessel to
dynamically adjust speed, thrust, and steering in response to currents, wind, or obstacles.
Additionally, CFD-driven weight distribution studies could refine the craft’s center of gravity and
buoyancy. Multiphase simulations analyzing cargo placement, battery positioning, and outrigger geometry
might reveal configurations that further reduce drag or enhance stability in rough waters. Coupled with
topology optimization, this could inform lightweight, 3D-printed structural components (e.g., carbon fiberreinforced mounts) to replace bulkier aluminum or PVC parts. These advancements, grounded in iterative
testing and computational modeling, would position The Nauti Buoy as a platform for cutting-edge research
in sustainable marine propulsion.REFERENCES

[1] United States Environmental Protection Agency. Air Pollution Emissions Overview. 2023. Accessed:
August 2023. Available: https://www.epa.gov/air-emissions-inventories/air-pollutionemissions-overview.
[2] Çengel, Y. A., and Boles, M. A. Thermodynamics: An Engineering Approach. 9th ed., McGraw-Hill
Education, 2019.
[3] Heywood, J. B. Internal Combustion Engine Fundamentals. 2nd ed., McGraw-Hill, 2018.

increased to 82.7N due to the outrigger-induced turbulence. The peak pressure at the bow of the boat rose by 18%, while flow separation at the stern diminished. This 25% drag increase necessitated reevaluation
of propulsion requirements. The team selected two Blue Robotics T200 thrusters (14.8lbf each, 65.8 N) to
deliver 131.7 N of total thrust, exceeding the revised minimum requirement of 82.7N (18.6lbf) and
ensuring robust performance under variable conditions.

2.2.THE PROPULSION SYSTEM (Integration)
Following the updated CFD analysis for the modified hull, the team chose two T200 Blue Robotics
Thrusters for propulsion. To optimize thrust efficiency and reduce unnecessary weight, the team has revised
the original mounting configuration for the thrusters. Instead of utilizing a back mount, the thrusters will
now be attached beneath the sealed, hollow 4-inch PVC outriggers, which are connected to the hull via
rectangular aluminum tubing. This strategic placement ensures proper thruster spacing, prevents thrust
interference and improves overall propulsion effectiveness. Additionally, this placement allows the team to
maximize the available space on the hull, which is particularly important given the compact size of the
vessel.
This design adjustment offers several key advantages. Firstly, eliminating the back mount reduces excess
structural weight, contributing to an improved thrust-to-weight ratio. Secondly, the lower positioning of the
thrusters within the water column enhances directional control and propulsion efficiency, minimizing
surface turbulence and energy loss.2.3.THE CONTROL SYSTEM
The Tidal Titans' electric watercraft integrates a robust control system based on sound engineering
principles to achieve real-time controllability and optimal power management. Figure 5 presents a System
Block Diagram of the control system.
Figure 5. System Block Diagram
The system employs a Radiolink transmitter and receiver as the primary control interface, making use of
closed-loop signal processing to ensure precise motor command execution with minimal latency. Power
delivery is following a strictly engineered plan, with propulsion coming from a 24V primary battery through
an isolated high-current bus and isolated 12V lithium batteries separately powering control and cooling to
preclude ground interaction and enhance reliability.
Voltage regulation is controlled through a high-efficiency buck converter with dynamic load compensation

to supply stable power with high rates of current changes. The drive system for the thrusters utilizes fieldoriented control software electronic speed controllers, housed in high-current XT90 connectors to reduce
power loss and react instantaneously to signal inputs. Thermally sensitive switching logic powers cooling
fans strategically placed to maintain optimal operating temperatures by utilizing calculated airflow patterns
taking into account component layout and heat dissipation rates.
Every aspect of hardware build shows consideration engineering. The IP67-rated weatherproof housing not

only protects against the environment but also incorporates shielding to keep electromagnetic interference to a minimum. Cabling within the unit follows best practice in high-vibration environments, with major
signal routes separated to reduce crosstalk. Parallel power supply with derating accommodates all the
components operating within safe tolerances, and the modular design facilitates simple maintenance and
fault location.
This system is an example of balanced electromechanical design, where theoretical principles—whether
Kirchhoff's circuit laws or thermal dynamics—are employed to achieve strong, competition-level
performance. The result is a watercraft that demonstrates how foundational engineering principles, when
properly applied, can yield straightforward solutions to what could have been tough technical challenges.
2.4. THE BATTERY MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (BMS)
The development of an efficient and reliable power system is essential for the performance of the
autonomous vessel. The BMS plays a critical role in monitoring battery health, ensuring safe operation, and
optimizing power delivery to meet the propulsion system's demands. This report presents a comprehensive
analysis of the selected battery, its integration with propulsion components, and the supporting electrical
systems necessary for safe and effective operation.
A LiFePO4 battery was chosen due to its superior cycle life, thermal stability, and high energy efficiency
compared to other lithium-ion chemistries. The Newport 24V 50Ah battery was selected for its ability to
deliver sufficient power to meet the propulsion system's energy demands. With the propulsion system
requiring approximately 737W to maintain the target speed of 15 mph, the Newport battery's 1.2
kWh energy capacity ensures the vessel can sustain this output for the duration of the race. This capacity
also provides an energy buffer to account for unexpected fluctuations in load or environmental conditions.
The battery's integrated BMS enhances system reliability with built-in protection features such as
overcharge, over-discharge, and overcurrent protection, safeguarding the system from power
inconsistencies that could impact performance. The BMS also ensures proper cell balancing, maintaining
even voltage distribution to maximize energy efficiency and extend battery life. Its temperature monitoring
system further prevents overheating by adjusting performance to maintain safe thermal conditions during
prolonged operation. These combined features ensure the battery can reliably support the propulsion
system, contributing to stable performance throughout the competition.
3. CAD and TESTING
A Computer-Aided design model was developed using Autodesk Fusion 360 for design, planning, and

simulation purposes. The RC boat hull was captured and created in the CAD model visually by referencing different image views of the actual hull. Once the RC hull was captured in the 3D model, hull modification
components were added to the model by utilizing provided STEP files from manufacturers for the aluminum
railings, PVC pipes, L brackets, bolts, and T200 thrusters. Sourcing manufacturer STEP files allowed more
accurate planning of the design construction by allowing virtual tests and simulations prior to procurement.
This static stress simulation examines the structural integrity of an aluminum 6061 railing intended to secure
an outrigger to the main hull of a naval system. The simulation simplifies the overall design in order to
isolate and focus on the stress behavior of the railing under anticipated operational loads.
Figure 6. Static Stress Analysis of Aluminum 6061 Railings
Multiple simulations were run to observe the railings' performance under varying loads. Two principal
forces are used in Figure 5: a 250 N vertical load in the Z direction to replicate the weight of the outrigger,
and a 100 N horizontal force in the X direction to approximate the push from onboard motors installed
beneath the outriggers. The maximum stress observed is approximately 17.728 MPa, located near the joint
where the railing connects to the hull, suggesting this region bears the highest combined load. The
information from these simulations informed reinforcements needed at stress concentration points. The
aluminum brackets used in the design are capable of withstanding this stress without exceeding their yield
strength, ensuring structural integrity under these conditions.
Testing Plan for ASNE PEP Competition
To ensure the performance, reliability, and safety of our unmanned electric-propelled watercraft, a series of
critical tests have been conducted, with additional evaluations planned. Initial tests were performed in the
lab, where the thrusters were placed in separate buckets of water to assess their functionality and power

draw. Subsequent testing involved using the university's swimming pool to evaluate the fully assembled watercraft's efficiency, maneuverability, and structural integrity, ensuring compliance with competition
requirements.
Completed Tests:
1. Dryness Test
This test evaluated the boat's waterproofing by conducting a dry rehearsal. The hull was carefully inspected
for leaks or breaches in its waterproofing system. Any identified gaps or holes were sealed with epoxy to
maintain the boat's integrity. The hull successfully passed the test with no leaks detected.
2. Battery Management System (BMS) Testing
The BMS underwent extensive testing to confirm its ability to regulate voltage, prevent overcharging, and
manage thermal conditions. The step-down converter integration was assessed to ensure optimal power
delivery while minimizing energy losses. Real-time monitoring of the State of Charge (SOC) and State of
Health (SOH) will be conducted using diagnostic tools to optimize battery performance and lifespan overall.
3. Buoyancy and Stability Assessment
Buoyancy tests were carried out to confirm the vessel's ability to remain afloat under varying payloads.
Stability evaluations ensured the watercraft maintains an even keel, preventing capsizing under sudden
movements or external disturbances.
4. Control System and Remote Kill Switch Validation
The reliability of the remote kill switch was tested to verify its ability to immediately shut down propulsion
in emergency scenarios. Signal range and response time will be analyzed to ensure safe remote operation.
5. Structural Load and Stress Testing
The mechanical durability of mounting brackets, outriggers, and propulsion supports will be tested under
simulated forces. This will verify that all structural elements can withstand operational stresses without
failure.
6. Battery Performance and Endurance
A runtime assessment was performed to determine the battery efficiency under continuous operation. The
initial battery performance test involved connecting the two thrusters to the battery and placing them in
separate buckets of water to evaluate the system's setup and power draw. This preliminary test provided
valuable insights into the system’s ability to sustain peak performance throughout the race.
Tests to be completed by March 28th, 2025:7. Maneuverability and Steering Control
The propulsion system’s response to control inputs will be evaluated through a series of turning radius tests.
The effectiveness of differential thrust steering will be measured, ensuring precise navigation without the
need for a rudder. Data will be collected on agility and directional stability under various load conditions.
8. Speed and Acceleration Tests
The maximum achievable speed will be measured using GPS tracking. Acceleration tests will be conducted
to evaluate thrust efficiency and propulsion response. These results will inform potential optimizations in
power distribution and hull hydrodynamics.
9. Environmental and Temperature Testing
The system’s performance under varying temperatures and environmental conditions will be analyzed to
ensure reliability in different weather scenarios. Heat dissipation efficiency of the BMS and propulsion
system will be assessed to prevent overheating during prolonged operation. These comprehensive tests will
ensure the watercraft is competition-ready, optimizing safety, efficiency, and performance for the ASNE
PEP event.
4. RISK MANAGEMENT
The Nauti Buoy's design integrates a comprehensive risk management strategy that addresses structural,
electrical, hydrodynamic, and operational hazards through proactive engineering solutions and redundant
systems. Structural Risks were a primary concern due to the significant dynamic loads anticipated during

competition. To mitigate potential failures, the team conducted iterative FEA simulations on key loadbearing components, particularly the aluminum 6061 mounting brackets and PVC outrigger joints. These
simulations identified stress concentrations near fastener holes, which were addressed by incorporating
gasket sheets and switching to larger diameter fasteners to improve load distribution. Waterproofing
measures included epoxy-sealed joints, gasket sheets for thruster mounts, and buoyant PVC outriggers.
These solutions were validated through dedicated dryness and buoyancy tests to ensure the vessel’s
integrity.
Thermal Management was approached using both active and passive cooling methods. The LiFePO4
battery pack’s integrated BMS provides cell-level monitoring, ensuring thermal stability during operation.
Additionally, two redundant 12V fans, controlled by NTC thermistors, provide active cooling to prevent
overheating during prolonged operation. This cooling system was tested through continuous stress testing
in the lab, simulating conditions exceeding the race duration to confirm reliability.To enhance Operational Safety, the control system was equipped with both RF and hardwired emergency
kill switches, enabling immediate shutdown in case of system malfunctions or emergencies.
These combined measures effectively mitigate identified risks while ensuring multiple layers of protection
against unexpected failures. The team will conduct final validation during open-water testing, ensuring
system interactions remain stable and reliable under real-world race conditions.
5. NEXT STEPS
To further advance The Nauti Buoy’s performance and expand its applications in marine engineering,
several strategic enhancements could be pursued. Integrating rudders alongside the existing thruster-based
steering system presents an opportunity to reduce energy consumption during maneuvers. By offloading
directional control from thrusters to hydrodynamically optimized rudders, power could be reallocated to
propulsion, improving overall efficiency. Computational simulations could compare rudder configurations
to identify designs that minimize drag while maximizing responsiveness. Autonomy and AI-driven

navigation represent another critical frontier. Implementing machine learning algorithms trained on realworld hydrodynamic and environmental data could enable adaptive pathfinding, allowing the vessel to
dynamically adjust speed, thrust, and steering in response to currents, wind, or obstacles.
Additionally, CFD-driven weight distribution studies could refine the craft’s center of gravity and
buoyancy. Multiphase simulations analyzing cargo placement, battery positioning, and outrigger geometry
might reveal configurations that further reduce drag or enhance stability in rough waters. Coupled with

topology optimization, this could inform lightweight, 3D-printed structural components (e.g., carbon fiberreinforced mounts) to replace bulkier aluminum or PVC parts. These advancements, grounded in iterative
testing and computational modeling, would position The Nauti Buoy as a platform for cutting-edge research
in sustainable marine propulsion.REFERENCES
